title: A living cell running on a quadruplet genetic code

concept.text: Millennium Problems for Biology 5, The quadruplet cell. Target: a living, replicating cell in which all protein-coding sequences, including the translation machinery, use uninterrupted, nonoverlapping four-base codons, a genuine quadruplet encoding rather than one where the first three positions determine the amino acid. Sources given: https://millenniumproblems.bio/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to BIO on 2026-11-15.
change_log.reason: One of the twelve Millennium Problems for Biology (Sam Rodriques and Michaela Hinks, FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, 2026), each with a stated concrete target; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: A living cell with an all-quadruplet genetic code
page.definition: A living, replicating cell uses four-base codons—nucleotide words specifying amino acids—for every protein. All four positions contribute to amino-acid identity, and no triplet decoding is detectable.

goal.need: Triplet codons provide 64 nucleotide words; quadruplets provide 256. An all-quadruplet cell would test whether a reproducing organism can use a different codon length and provide additional assignments for amino acids beyond the usual 20. The 2022 study identifies competition with triplet translation as a barrier.

figures.caption: Coding capacity with four nucleotide letters
figures.note: These are sequence combinations, not demonstrated amino-acid assignments.

statements.quote: Produce a living cell that uses a four-base codon code.
statements.context: Millennium Problems for Biology, problem 05, contributed by Erika Alden DeBenedictis.

statements.body: MIT–Yale quadruplet-code research team: DeBenedictis, Söll and Esvelt
statements.quote: These data provide a blueprint for synthetic biologists to deliberately engineer an all-quadruplet expanded genetic code.

completion.title: A replicating cell uses a genuine quadruplet code for every protein.
completion.criterion: A living, replicating cell encodes every protein-coding sequence, including translation machinery, as uninterrupted, nonoverlapping quadruplet codons, without detectable triplet decoding. Mutations have similar probabilities of changing the encoded amino acid at all four positions. Codes whose first three positions always or almost always determine the amino acid fail.
completion.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, Millennium Problems for Biology, problem 05 acceptance criteria.
completion.threshold_quote: encoded as uninterrupted nonoverlapping quadruplet codons, without detectable triplet decoding.
completion.basis: Problem 05 supplies the whole-cell acceptance test. It gives no numerical interpretation of detectable or similar.

milestones.title: A cell-free system makes an active protein by decoding a four-base codon.
milestones.criterion: A cell-free system produces a full-length, enzymatically active protein despite a four-base codon replacing a triplet. Ma et al., published on 10 August 1993, demonstrated this with dihydrofolate reductase in an Escherichia coli transcription–translation extract. The accessible abstract gives no replicate count.
milestones.set_by: Ma et al., Biochemistry (1993), published cell-free protein-synthesis assay endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: The results indicate that all four synthetic tRNAs were functionally active in the synthesis of full-length, enzymatically active dihydrofolate reductase protein.

milestones.title: Living cells decode four distinct quadruplet codons in one protein.
milestones.criterion: A living Escherichia coli cell produces full-length green fluorescent protein from a reporter containing four distinct quadruplet codons, with the intended amino acids confirmed by mass spectrometry. Published on 29 September 2021: fluorescence was 0.45% of the triplet-coded control; n = 20 biologically independent samples.
milestones.set_by: DeBenedictis et al., Nature Communications (2021), Figure 5 demonstration endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: four unique quadruplet codons by their corresponding qtRNAs in a single reporter.

milestones.title: Quadruplet decoding of an endogenous gene restores respiratory growth in yeast.
milestones.criterion: Quadruplet decoding restores full-length COX3, a respiratory-chain protein, and growth of Saccharomyces cerevisiae on nonfermentable carbon sources. Published on 4 December 2024: the tryptophan-decoding strain doubled in 4.1 hours versus 3.4 hours for the wild-type control; n = 4 per condition. Only one codon in the mitochondrial gene was changed.
milestones.set_by: Pigula, Ban and Schultz, ACS Synthetic Biology (2024), Figures 2–3; this assay applies to yeast mitochondria.
milestones.threshold_quote: growth on nonfermentable media containing ethanol and glycerol as carbon sources (YPEG).

milestones.title: A quadruplet translation system incorporates all 20 standard protein amino acids.
milestones.criterion: Quadruplet codons direct incorporation of all 20 standard protein amino acids. The authors describe this as a presumed prerequisite for an all-quadruplet code. Their paper, published on 16 March 2022, counts nine compatible amino-acid charging enzymes. The amino-acid identity measurements in Figure 5 used one biological replicate per measured variant.
milestones.set_by: DeBenedictis, Söll and Esvelt, eLife (2022), Introduction; a proposed prerequisite for retaining the standard 20-amino-acid repertoire.
milestones.threshold_quote: 20 canonical amino acids directed by quadruplet codons.

milestones.title: A cell replicates with every protein-coding sequence encoded in quadruplets.
milestones.criterion: A cell reproduces with every protein-coding sequence, including translation machinery, encoded as uninterrupted, nonoverlapping quadruplets. Decoding specificity remains unestablished. No qualifying result was found.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback after searches of challenge criteria, quadruplet-code papers and government roadmaps found no penultimate test; retains problem 05's replication and genome-encoding components.

not_found: No external staged roadmap defining a penultimate whole-cell acceptance test was found.
Problem 05 specifies no numerical detection limit, tolerance for similar mutation probabilities, or minimum replication duration.
No published result satisfying the whole-cell completion criterion was found.
The 1993 paper's full text could not be opened; its PubMed abstract reports no sample size.
